title: Occasion and date
short: Written at Stoke Poges in August 1742, two months after the death of Gray's closest friend, Richard West, on 1 June 1742.
body: Richard West (1716-1742), Gray's friend from Eton, was a poet in poor health who died of consumption at 25. Gray had sent him his 'Ode on the Spring' without knowing he was dying. Gray's fair copy in his Commonplace Book is headed 'Sonnet' and dated 'at Stoke, Aug: 1742'; he did not publish it, and it first appeared in William Mason's edition of Gray's Poems with his Memoirs (1775). Gray also mourned West in his unfinished Latin poem De Principiis Cogitandi, addressed to 'Favonius' (usually identified with West), which breaks off in a lament for him. The text here keeps Gray's own older spellings (redning, joyn, chearful).

title: Rhyme scheme and turn
short: The volta comes at l. 9; the sestet repeats the octave's images of morning, birds and fields, now as they are for other men.
body: The sonnet was rare in English between Milton and Gray, and Gray's is one of the few of the mid-century. The octave alternates two rhymes throughout (shine / Fire / joyn / Attire / repine / require / mine / expire), an Italian economy of rhyme in an alternating pattern; the sestet alternates two more (chear / Men / bear / complain / hear / vain). The 'Yet' of l. 9 turns from the speaker's grief to the world's indifference. Its design, nature renewing itself while the mourner cannot, belongs to an old elegiac topos found in Petrarch's sonnet 'Zephiro torna' (Rime 310), to which the sonnet has often been compared.

title: smiling Mornings
short: A Miltonic phrase: Milton's 'smiling morn' occurs in Paradise Lost, as Gray's nineteenth-century editors noted.
body: Bradshaw (1891) points out three instances of the 'smiling morn' in Paradise Lost (v.124, v.168, xi.175). The personified smiling morning is a stock of eighteenth-century descriptive diction and is precisely the sort of phrase Wordsworth would object to as 'poetic diction'. The plural 'Mornings' makes the joy of nature recur day after day, which heightens the speaker's isolation. The phrase returns in l. 9 ('Yet Morning smiles'), the hinge of the sonnet.

title: redning Phoebus
short: Phoebus Apollo, the sun god; 'redning' (reddening) describes the dawn sky as the sun rises.
body: Phoebus, 'the bright one', is the epithet of Apollo as sun god, a classical periphrasis for the sun. 'Lifts his golden Fire' completes the image of sunrise. 'Redning' is Gray's own spelling of 'reddening'. Wordsworth singled out this kind of mythological ornament as artificial; defenders have answered that Gray deliberately sets the conventional splendour of the octave's first lines against the plain statements of grief that follow.

title: amorous Descant
short: Descant is a melody or song, properly a part sung above a plainsong; the phrase is taken from Milton's nightingale.
body: In music a descant is an ornamental melody sung above a fixed tune (Medieval Latin discantus). Milton's nightingale in Paradise Lost 'all night long her amorous descant sung' (Bradshaw cites iv.603, Tovey iv.602). Tovey adds that 'descant' in Milton means a variation on a plain song, a precision Gray's general application to birdsong loses. 'Joyn' is Gray's spelling of 'join'. The birds' love-song is one of three images (sun, birds, fields) that the sestet takes up again.

title: green Attire
short: The fields put on their spring clothing again, a personification Milton also used ('Earth in her rich attire').
body: Bradshaw compares Paradise Lost vii.501, 'Earth in her rich attire'. 'Resume' implies the yearly renewal of nature after winter, which is the root of the poem's contrast between cyclical natural time and the finality of human death. The 'chearful Fields' (Gray's spelling) are personified as capable of cheerfulness, an attribution the speaker cannot share. Gray's three images in the opening quatrain (sun, birds, fields) are deliberately conventional, the common furniture of spring poems, and the sestet will return to each in turn to show that the world's renewal continues for others while the speaker is shut out from it.

title: repine
short: To repine is to fret or long discontentedly; his ears long for 'other Notes', the voice of his dead friend.
body: The OED gives 'repine' as to feel or express discontent, to fret, and also to long for something with discontent. 'Notes' plays on the birds' notes of l. 3 and the human voice of West, perhaps also his poetry. Ears and eyes in ll. 5-6 shift the poem from the outward scene to the bodily senses of the mourner, which find nothing they want in nature.

title: Wordsworth's critique
short: Wordsworth printed this sonnet in his 1800 Preface, italicising ll. 6-8 and 13-14 as its only valuable lines; Coleridge disputed him.
body: In the Preface to Lyrical Ballads (1800) Wordsworth used the sonnet to attack poetic diction. He set ll. 6-8 and 13-14 in italics and declared that 'the only part of this Sonnet which is of any value' was those lines, whose language differs from prose only in rhyme and in 'fruitless' for 'fruitlessly'. Coleridge replied in Biographia Literaria ch. 18 that the distinction between prose and metrical language is real, and found faults in the italicised lines too. Foladare (1960) re-examined the charge that the sonnet is stilted and asked how well its emotion is actually concealed; the contrast of conventional and plain diction can be read as part of Gray's design, the ornate lines belonging to the world's joy and the plain ones to the mourner.

title: imperfect
short: Imperfect means incomplete: without West to share them, his joys cannot be completed and die in his breast.
body: Bradshaw glosses 'imperfect' as incomplete, because the joys cannot be shared with the friend. The scansion requires elision ('th'imperfect'). Rogers compared Dryden's 'And in my ear the imperfect accent dies', which Tovey thought a parallel in rhythm rather than thought. The line closes the octave on 'expire', a word that also means to die, so that the joys share the fate of the friend.

title: the busy Race
short: Busy mankind, at work and occupied with the cares of life, whom morning still cheers.
body: 'Race' is the human race; 'busy' suggests both industry and the distraction of the living from death. The phrase anticipates the 'happier Men' of l. 10 and, in Gray's later work, the 'busy' world from which the dead of the Elegy are absent (the housewife 'busy' at her evening care). The sestet thus generalises: the world goes on, and the one person who would share the speaker's sense of loss is gone.

title: wonted Tribute
short: Wonted means customary, usual; the fields pay their accustomed tribute of harvest to all.
body: 'Wonted' (from the old verb 'won', to dwell, be accustomed) is a poetic archaism in Gray's day. 'Tribute' figures the crops as a payment owed by the fields to mankind, a georgic conception. 'To all' is pointed: the speaker alone receives nothing from nature's generosity. The line recalls the language of Virgil's Georgics and its English imitators, in which the earth pays its yearly dues to the farmer; the economic metaphor stresses regularity and reliability, exactly what death has removed from the speaker's own life.

title: complain
short: To complain is to sing a lover's lament; the birds sing to warm, that is to woo, their 'little Loves', their mates.
body: In amorous poetry 'complain' meant to utter a love-plaint, a sense the OED records; birdsong was imagined as courtship. 'To warm their little Loves' means to make their mates ardent, and the diminutive is affectionate. The line renews the 'amorous Descant' of l. 3, and the plaintive verb 'complain' anticipates the speaker's own lament in the next line, whose object, unlike theirs, 'cannot hear'.

title: fruitless
short: An adjective used as an adverb, 'fruitlessly'; Wordsworth noted it as one of the few unprosaic touches in the lines he praised.
body: Gray's use of 'fruitless' adverbially is a Latinate, poetic licence. It contrasts with the fields' 'Tribute' just before: the fields bear fruit, the mourner's grief does not. The line's plain statement ('to him that cannot hear') is the emotional centre of the sonnet, and Wordsworth italicised it as such. 'To him that cannot hear' points back to the 'other Notes' of l. 5: the ears that longed for West's voice now address a friend who cannot hear them, so the poem's address itself becomes a sign of loss. Coleridge, by contrast, found even the italicised lines open to criticism.

title: weep in vain
short: The paradox (weeping more because weeping is useless) has classical roots in an anecdote of Solon and an English source in Cibber's Richard III.
body: Bradshaw and Tovey both cite Colley Cibber's adaptation of Richard III (the two editors give the line in slightly different wordings). Bradshaw also recalls the anecdote of Solon, who, told that weeping for his dead son would avail nothing, replied that he wept precisely for that reason; he notes a similar story of Augustus. Tovey cites Diogenes Laertius for Solon. The last line returns to the poem's first words, 'In vain', closing the sonnet in a ring and turning the futility of nature's joys into the futility of grief.
